lines.text: A customer hid one sentence in a chat message.
Three agents later, fifty thousand rupees were about to leave.
Gjallarhorn caught it mid-air.
Lock a rogue agent in under two milliseconds.
Let an AI co-pilot write the fix, and prove it first.
Thirty-one attacks. Zero harm.
Let me show you how.
Teams now run many AI agents. They call models, use tools, and ask each other for help.
When one of them is tricked, today's gateways can't tell you which agent did it, who asked whom, or whether a permission was borrowed.
OWASP calls that last one a confused deputy.
lines.say: Oh-wasp calls that last one a confused deputy.

lines.text: Gjallarhorn is a plugin for the Bifrost AI gateway that answers all three, on every call.
lines.say: Yallarhorn is a plugin for the Bifrost AI gateway that answers all three, on every call.

lines.text: This is the live console. Every flight is a real call crossing the gateway, between people, agents, tools and models.
Here's an attack. A customer message tells the support agent to get a refund. Support isn't allowed to refund, so it asks the billing agent, which is.
Bifrost allows every hop. Gjallarhorn sees the whole chain, and the refund stops mid-air.
lines.say: Bifrost allows every hop. Yallarhorn sees the whole chain, and the refund stops mid-air.

lines.text: One click opens the incident: the chain from the customer chat, through support, to billing, and the rule that stopped it.
The AI co-pilot explains it in plain words, using only facts from the flight recorder.
If an agent misbehaves, I can lock it. Billing is cut off from models, tools and other agents on its very next call, and the people it works for keep their access.
We measured it. The next call is refused a median of one point eight milliseconds after the lock.
No policy is perfect. Here I remove the rule that stops outside chains from sending email.
The replay check calls it safe, because nothing recorded needed that rule. So I save.
Now a forum post tricks an agent into emailing customer data out. This time, harm is done.
I find the call in the table, open it, and ask the co-pilot for a rule.
It doesn't trust its own ideas. Every suggestion is replayed against all the traffic we recorded.
These three are proven safe.
Six were rejected on their own: five would block normal work, and one was malformed.
I apply a proven rule, and the server proves it again before switching it on.
Same attack, one more time. Blocked.
Every decision lands in a hash-chained flight recorder. I can replay the last minute of traffic,
open any agent, browse every call in the table, and test a policy change against real traffic before I save it.
Under the hood, Gjallarhorn is a Go plugin that Bifrost loads through its official hooks. Bifrost isn't forked.
lines.say: Under the hood, Yallarhorn is a Go plugin that Bifrost loads through its official hooks. Bifrost isn't forked.

lines.text: When one agent calls another, the gateway signs a chain ticket. Agents can drop it, but they can't forge it.
Every model, tool and agent call is checked against lockdowns and policy, in about fifty microseconds, and every decision is recorded.
To prove it, we built an attack lab: thirty-one attacks through the real gateway.
Without Gjallarhorn, twelve of them caused real harm. With it, none did.
lines.say: Without Yallarhorn, twelve of them caused real harm. With it, none did.

lines.text: All eleven pieces of normal work still got done, with zero false blocks.
Every number links to its raw result file, and the threat model says plainly what Gjallarhorn does not protect against.
lines.say: Every number links to its raw result file, and the threat model says plainly what Yallarhorn does not protect against.

lines.text: It's open source. Clone the repo, run one command, and launch an attack yourself.
Gjallarhorn. The horn that warns you when your agents go wrong.
lines.say: Yallarhorn. The horn that warns you when your agents go wrong.
